name: Guptar Ghat
description: A 19th-century ghat 10 km downstream from Ayodhya Junction where the Valmiki Ramayana places Lord Ram's Jal Samadhi — the moment he walked into the Saryu and returned to Vaikuntha. King Darshan Singh of Bharatpur built the present stone steps in the early 1800s. The Sita-Ram, Chakrahari and Narsingh shrines line the bathing platform; the river bends here so the water is calmer and clearer than at Ram Ki Paidi.
why_hidden: Tour operators run shuttles between Ram Mandir, Hanuman Garhi and Sarayu Aarti — Guptar Ghat is 10 km out of the way and gets skipped by all but the most thorough Ramayana-circuit pilgrims.
best_time: October to March, mornings 6-8 AM for the calmest river and softest light
how_to_reach: 10 km from Ayodhya Junction by road via NH-330 toward Faizabad cantonment; auto or e-rickshaw from old Ayodhya costs ₹150-250 round trip. The ghat sits inside the Cantonment area — keep ID handy.
tips: Free entry. No facilities or food stalls — eat in town first. Photography permitted on the steps. Combine with a stop at Choti Devkali Temple en route. Avoid monsoon (Jul-Sep) when the Saryu submerges the lower steps.

name: Bharat Kund, Nandigram
description: A pond and 14th-century temple complex 19 km south of Ayodhya in Nandigram village, where Bharat ruled Kosala for 14 years with Ram's wooden padukas placed on the throne in his stead. The Hanuman-Bharat Milap Mandir marks the spot where Hanuman first brought news of Ram's return. Bharat is said to have bathed in this very kund through the entire exile period.
why_hidden: Nandigram has no organised tourism — no restaurants, no signage in English, no shuttles from Ayodhya. The Ramayana-circuit shuttle bus runs only the inner-city loop, and 99% of pilgrims never make it the 19 km south.
best_time: October to March, mornings; daily evening aarti is reportedly held at Bharat Kund
how_to_reach: 19 km south of Ayodhya in Sohawal tehsil, off the Ayodhya-Sultanpur road. Hire a taxi (₹800-1200 round trip with wait) or self-drive — public transport is unreliable. Allow 2-4 hours.
tips: No restaurants in Nandigram — pack water and snacks. Free entry. Modest dress. Locals point out the kund, the Bharat-Hanuman Milap Mandir, and a neem tree said to mark Bharat's hut. Combine with Surya Kund (4 km from old Ayodhya) on the return drive.

name: Husainabad Picture Gallery (Baradari)
description: An 1838 summer baradari built by Nawab Mohammad Ali Shah, the third Nawab of Awadh, that now houses the only complete set of life-size Awadh Nawab portraits — from Saadat Khan to Wajid Ali Shah. The portraits were painted between 1882-1885 by European artists Dawling, Gravet and Harrison plus Indian painter D.S. Singh. The figures appear to follow you across the room, their eyes locked at every angle.
why_hidden: Visitors flock to the adjacent Chota Imambara and Clock Tower and walk straight past the picture gallery's plain doorway. Most guidebooks bury it as a footnote — yet this is where Awadhi history is told face-by-face.
best_time: October to March, weekdays 10 AM to 4 PM to avoid weekend tour crowds
how_to_reach: Inside the Husainabad complex, 50 metres from the Chota Imambara entrance. Auto from Hazratganj is ₹100-150. Walk-in via the Husainabad Bazaar lane.
tips: Entry ₹25-50 Indian / ₹200 foreign. Photography strictly prohibited inside — guards enforce it. Closed Fridays. Allow 30-45 minutes. The Hussainabad Clock Tower (1881) and Talaab next door round out the half-day.

name: Constantia House (Claude Martin's Tomb), La Martiniere
description: The largest European funerary monument in India, built 1785-1800 by Major-General Claude Martin — a French soldier who arrived in India as a private and died one of Awadh's wealthiest men. He willed the building to be his mausoleum, and his coffin still rests in a vaulted chamber 18 feet below the central tower. The Indo-European facade — flying lions, classical columns, gothic arches — has no parallel in India. La Martiniere College, founded 1840, has run inside it ever since.
why_hidden: It is an active boys' boarding school, so casual visitors aren't expected. Tourists detour to Bara Imambara and skip the 4 km drive south. Yet the basement vault is open to respectful visitors and the architecture is the most eccentric building in north India.
best_time: October to March; weekdays after school hours (4 PM onward) or weekends with prior phone permission
how_to_reach: La Martiniere Boys' College, La Martiniere Road, 4 km south of Hazratganj. Auto/cab ₹150-200. Enter via the main gate; visitors must sign in at the security post.
tips: Call the school office ahead (0522-2235451) before turning up — access depends on day and event calendar. Free entry but a small donation to the school upkeep fund is customary. Photography of exteriors only. The basement crypt with Martin's tomb is reached via a stair behind the central hall — ask a peon to unlock.

name: Bhardwaj Ashram, Colonelganj
description: An active ashram and 100+ Shiva-linga complex in the Colonelganj/George Town neighbourhood, identified in the Ramcharitmanas as the place where Sage Bhardwaj welcomed Ram, Sita and Lakshman on their way to Chitrakoot. The Bhardwajeshwar Linga at the centre is said to have been consecrated by the rishi himself. A grand statue of Maharshi Bhardwaj was installed in the adjoining park before the 2019 Kumbh.
why_hidden: Pilgrims peel off straight to the Sangam after Anand Bhawan; Bhardwaj Ashram sits 2 km west and is missed by the standard taxi circuit despite being one of the oldest continuously worshipped sites in the city.
best_time: October to February, mornings 6-9 AM; especially Maha Shivratri and during Kumbh/Magh Mela bathing days
how_to_reach: Near Swaraj Bhavan, Colonelganj, George Town, Prayagraj 211002 — about 3 km from Prayagraj Junction. Auto from the station ₹80-120; from Sangam ₹150.
tips: Free entry. Open dawn to dusk. Modest dress. The Bhardwaj Park opposite has the Maharshi statue and benches if you want a quiet hour. Combine with Anand Bhawan (1.5 km) on the same loop. Avoid Kumbh main bathing days unless you're there for the mela itself — crowds become unmanageable.

name: Mankameshwar Temple, Saraswati Ghat
description: An ancient Shiva temple on the Yamuna's right bank in the Cantonment, housing a 3.5-foot black-stone Shivalinga that local tradition says Lord Ram installed for Sita on the way to Chitrakoot. The temple is mentioned by name in the Shiva Purana, Padma Purana and Skanda Purana as 'Kameshwar Tirtha'. The riverside aarti at sunset draws fewer than fifty regulars on most days — the antithesis of the Sangam crowd.
why_hidden: It sits inside the Cantonment area, so taxis don't loop here automatically. Most pilgrims have already done their Yamuna-Ganga snan at Sangam and don't realise the city's oldest Shivalinga is upstream.
best_time: October to February; daily 5 AM-12 PM and 3-9 PM. Maha Shivratri and Sawan Mondays are biggest
how_to_reach: Saraswati Ghat, near Old Cantonment area, ~3 km from Prayagraj Junction. Auto/e-rickshaw ₹80-120. Walk down the ghat steps from the Cantt road.
tips: Free entry. No footwear inside. Photography of the courtyard is fine; not the garbhagriha. Combine with a Saraswati Ghat boat ride (₹100-300 share). Modest dress; head covered in the inner sanctum is appreciated.

name: Kalatop Wildlife Sanctuary Trek
description: A 30.7 sq-km deodar and oak forest sanctuary 12 km from Dalhousie, holding leopard, Himalayan black bear, goral, serow, barking deer and the Eurasian/black-headed jay. The classic walk — Lakkar Mandi to the Forest Rest House and back, 8 km return — climbs through dense conifers with snow-peak windows on the upper ridge. The 1925 Forest Rest House (bookable through DFO Chamba) lets you overnight inside the protected zone.
why_hidden: Khajjiar's Mini-Switzerland meadow gets every postcard. Kalatop, just down the same road, gets the day-trippers who skip the meadow — a much smaller crowd.
best_time: March to May for rhododendron and clear ridge views; September to November for crisp air after monsoon
how_to_reach: From Dalhousie, drive 8 km to Lakkar Mandi (taxi ₹600-900 one way). Park, register at the forest gate, and walk 4 km to the Rest House through the sanctuary trail.
tips: Entry ~₹100 Indian / ₹400 foreigner; vehicle entry ₹200 extra. Open 7 AM-5 PM; arrive before 9 AM for wildlife. Carry ID, cash and water — no shops inside. A guide (₹500-800) is recommended after dusk and if you want to spot leopard sign. Forest Rest House booking: DFO Chamba office, prior written permission required.

name: Dainkund Peak (Singing Hill) & Pholani Devi Temple
description: At 2,755 metres, the highest point near Dalhousie. Wind through the deodar-pine-oak ridge produces a low whistling drone that gives the peak its 'Singing Hill' name. The summit holds the small Pholani Devi shrine — no idol, only a trishul — and a 360-degree view of the Pir Panjal, Dhauladhar and Chamba Valley. The 4.5 km trail from the Indian Air Force gate is well-marked and graded.
why_hidden: Most weekenders stop at the IAF gate viewpoint and turn around without doing the trek to the actual summit shrine. The trail is on a restricted Air Force road, so commercial operators don't push it.
best_time: March-June and September-November; clear days deliver the Pir Panjal panorama. Avoid monsoon for slip risk and winter for snow blockage
how_to_reach: Drive 10 km from Dalhousie via Lakkar Mandi to the IAF Dainkund gate (taxi ₹500-700). Park there; the trail starts at the gate barrier. 4.5 km / 2-3 hours one way to the summit shrine.
tips: Free entry; trail is shared with IAF personnel — no photography of military installations. Carry water, layers and a windcheater (the ridge is exposed). Trekking shoes recommended. No food on the trail. Combine with Kalatop on the same day if you start early.

name: Christ Church (1844)
description: An Anglican Neo-Gothic church whose foundation stone was laid by Bishop Daniel Wilson of Calcutta on 26 October 1844. The Spanish and Italian stained glass — Christ, Mary, St Barnabas and St Francis above the altar — survives intact. The 1890 W.H. Bailey & Co. pipe organ is one of the few still playable in India. The clock tower clock was imported from Manchester. The CNI Diocese of Amritsar runs the church today; Sunday service in English continues unbroken.
why_hidden: Mall Road and Monkey Point dominate the Kasauli itinerary. Christ Church is on the Lower Mall, often passed at speed by tourists who don't realise the organ and stained glass are 19th-century originals — and that the building still functions as a working Anglican church.
best_time: April to June and September to November; Sunday service 10 AM (English) for the organ; weekdays 9 AM-5 PM for quiet visits
how_to_reach: Lower Mall, Kasauli, 1 km from the Bus Stand. Walking distance from the Upper Mall via the connecting path. No vehicles inside the cantonment beyond the parking lots.
tips: Free entry; donations to the Church of North India fund welcomed. Modest dress. Photography of exteriors and stained glass usually permitted; ask before photographing the altar. Quiet voices inside even when service isn't on. Combine with the 4 km Lower Mall walk to the Manki Point trail.

name: Kasauli Brewery & Distillery (Mohan Meakin)
description: The oldest operating distillery in Asia, founded by Edward Dyer in the 1820s-1850s using mountain spring water that he judged similar to the Scottish Highlands. The brewery moved to Solan in the 1880s when Kasauli town began drawing the same springs; the original Kasauli site stayed as a distillery. Mohan Meakin Ltd has run it since 1949. India's first single malt — Solan No. 1 — and Asia's first beer brand, Lion Beer, both originated here.
why_hidden: It is a working industrial site, not a tourist attraction — there is no formal visitor centre. Most travellers don't know the distillery exists, let alone that it predates every other operating malt-maker in Asia.
best_time: April to June and September to November; weekdays only, working hours 10 AM-4 PM
how_to_reach: Lower Mall, Kasauli, just below the bus stand and Christ Church. The compound boundary is visible from the Mall walking path; main gate is on the access road.
tips: No public tours and no on-site retail outlet — visits are at the discretion of the staff and usually require prior written permission via Mohan Meakin's office (Solan or Ghaziabad HQ). Most travellers settle for the heritage signage and the boundary-wall view. Don't trespass — it is an active liquor manufacturing facility with security.

name: Jhirna Zone Year-Round Safari
description: The southernmost safari zone of Corbett, opened year-round (unlike Bijrani/Dhikala which shut in monsoon). Entry is via Dhela Gate, 15 km from Ramnagar. The terrain is open grassland and dry deciduous scrub — better for sloth bear and gaur sightings than the canonical tiger zones. Maximum 30 jeeps per shift, so the bookings cap stops the safari-traffic-jam problem that hits Bijrani in peak season.
why_hidden: Every first-timer asks for Dhikala or Bijrani. Jhirna gets the leftover and the monsoon-month travellers — which means smaller crowds and a near-guarantee of seeing sloth bear, the species Corbett under-promotes.
best_time: Open 365 days. November-February is peak; July-September is the only zone running during monsoon (booked day-of, not in advance)
how_to_reach: Dhela Gate, 15 km southeast of Ramnagar via the Kalagarh road. Self-drive to the gate; the safari jeep + naturalist is mandatory inside. Online booking via the Uttarakhand Forest Department portal opens 45-60 days ahead.
tips: Day permit ₹600-1,500 Indian / ₹2,500-4,000 foreign + jeep ₹2,500-3,500 + guide ₹600 — total around ₹4,000-6,500 for 2 people. Two shifts daily: 6-10 AM and 12-4 PM. Carry binoculars; sloth bears are the star but easily missed. Monsoon safaris are weather-dependent and may cancel mid-shift.

name: Jim Corbett's House & Kaladhungi Heritage Trail
description: Jim Corbett's actual home in Choti Haldwani, 2 km west of Kaladhungi on the Ramnagar road, where he and his sister Maggie wintered from 1922 onward. The bungalow is preserved as a small museum — his rifles, fishing tackle, photographs, the books he wrote here. The 3 km eco-trail through khair, sheesham and teak forest links the house to Corbett Falls, a 60-foot drop on a side stream. Local naturalists from the Choti Haldwani samiti guide the walk.
why_hidden: Travellers fly into safari camps and never drive west to Kaladhungi. The Jim Corbett 'museum' most people see is the small one inside Dhikala — the actual family home in Choti Haldwani is an hour's drive away and gets a fraction of the visitors.
best_time: October to April; mornings 8-10 AM for birding on the eco-trail
how_to_reach: Choti Haldwani / Kaladhungi, 26 km from Ramnagar. Self-drive or hired taxi (₹1,500-2,500 round trip from Corbett resorts). Combine with Corbett Falls (5 km further on the Nayagaon road).
tips: Museum entry ₹50 Indian / ₹100 foreign; closed Mondays; open 8 AM-5 PM. Eco-trail guide arranged through the Choti Haldwani Gram Vikas Samiti (~₹500-800). Carry water and a hat. Pair with Corbett Falls and the Boar Bridge over the Baur for a 4-5 hour half-day.

name: Chaubatia Government Apple Orchards
description: A 600-acre government fruit research centre 10 km south of Ranikhet at 1,800 metres, established in 1919 by the British colonial administration as a horticulture station. Today it grows over 200 varieties of apple, plum, peach, apricot and pear under the Uttarakhand Horticulture Department, with the open orchard rows on view to visitors. Lord Mayo, Viceroy in 1869-72, was so taken with the site that he ordered the British cavalry cantonment built next door.
why_hidden: Day-trippers head to Jhula Devi and Mall Road and never make the 10 km loop south. The orchard is government-run, not a commercial farmstay — there's no marketing budget, just a gate, a research office, and rows of fruit trees.
best_time: March-April for blossom; July-September for ripe peaches and plums; October-November for apples and clear Trishul views
how_to_reach: 10 km south of Ranikhet via the Chaubatia road. Taxi ₹400-700 round trip; or self-drive. The orchard gate has parking; entry through the visitor lane to the research office.
tips: Entry ~₹15-30 per head; open 8 AM-5 PM. Photography fine; do not pluck fruit. Government Garden Restaurant on site sells fresh apple juice and squash. Combine with the 2 km walk to Bhaludam viewpoint for the Nanda Devi-Trishul-Nandaghunti panorama.

name: Kumaon Regimental Centre Museum
description: A regimental military museum inside the Indian Army's Kumaon Regiment cantonment, set up in the 1970s to display the unit's record from 1862 onward. Holdings include silver scepters of Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi, captured 1962 Sino-Indian War rifles and Chinese radios, Kargil War documents, and stories of the regiment's two Param Vir Chakra recipients — Major Somnath Sharma (1947) and Captain Gurbachan Singh Salaria (1961). One of the most decorated regiments of the Indian Army.
why_hidden: Cantonment access requires ID at the gate, so casual tourists self-deselect. Holiday makers go to Jhula Devi and the golf course — the army museum is invisible on most travel-blog itineraries even though it sits 2 km from Mall Road.
best_time: March-June and September-November; weekdays 9 AM-5 PM (closed Wednesdays for maintenance)
how_to_reach: KRC Centre, Ranikhet Cantonment, 2 km from Mall Road. Taxi ₹150-250 one way. ID (Aadhaar/passport) mandatory at the cantonment gate.
tips: Entry ₹75 per head. Photography inside is restricted. Allow 60-90 minutes. Modest dress required (army cantonment). The 1947 PVC display and the Chinese-arms cabinet are the highlights — ask the on-duty soldier for a 5-minute walk-through if you want context.

name: Trevor's Tank Crocodile & Wildlife Sanctuary
description: A man-made reservoir 5 km from Mount Abu town, built in 1897 by British engineer Colonel G.H. Trevor for crocodile breeding. The tank still functions as an active mugger crocodile sanctuary. Stone-built viewing huts ring the shore for spotting crocodiles basking on the rocks plus peafowl, sloth bear, sambar and the occasional black panther in the surrounding forest.
why_hidden: Dilwara, Nakki Lake and Sunset Point soak up every Mount Abu day-tripper. Trevor's Tank is 5 km off the main loop, on a forest road that doesn't have organised tourist transport — so it stays quiet even on Saturday afternoons.
best_time: October to March, mornings 7-10 AM and afternoons 4-6 PM when crocodiles bask
how_to_reach: 5 km from Mount Abu town via the Oriya road. Taxi ₹300-500 round trip with wait, or rent a 2-wheeler in town. Last 500 m is a forest path — park at the gate.
tips: Entry ₹50-100 per head; open 9 AM-5 PM. Carry binoculars. Stay on marked paths — the embankment is not fenced and crocodiles can move out of the water. Combine with Achalgarh Fort (6 km further) for a half-day. Avoid monsoon when the trail is leech-prone.

name: Achalgarh Fort & Achaleshwar Mahadev Temple
description: An 11 km drive north of Mount Abu town to the 9th-century Achaleshwar Mahadev temple — a Paramara-dynasty Shiva shrine where the toe of the deity is worshipped instead of a linga. A four-tonne five-metal Nandi statue stands at the entrance. The fort wall above was rebuilt in 1452 by Maharana Kumbha as one of his 32 forts, with the Hanumanpol and Champapol gates still intact. Inside the compound: the 15th-century Kantinath Jain temple and the Mandakini Kund tank ringed by buffalo-sculptures and a Rajput-king image.
why_hidden: Coach tours run Dilwara → Nakki → Sunset Point and skip the 11 km drive north. Achalgarh has no entry counter, no shuttle, no signposts in Hindi-English-Marathi like Dilwara. It's a working temple inside fort ruins — exactly the kind of site that the volume tourism circuit ignores.
best_time: October to March; mornings 6-10 AM for puja and clear visibility on the Mandakini Kund
how_to_reach: 11 km north of Mount Abu via the Achalgarh road. Taxi ₹500-800 round trip with 2-hour wait, or self-drive. The temple is at the road end; the fort gates are a 5-minute climb above.
tips: Free entry to temple and fort. Footwear off in temple. Photography of the Nandi and outer fort is fine; not the inner garbhagriha. Combine with Trevor's Tank (6 km away) and Guru Shikhar (4 km further) for a north-loop half-day. Modest dress.

name: Charan Paduka Trek (Vishnu's Footprints)
description: A 3 km uphill trek from the left side of Badrinath temple to a rock at 3,380 metres bearing what local tradition holds are the footprints of Lord Vishnu. The view from the platform takes in Neelkanth Peak (6,597 m) on one side and Nar Parvat on the other, with the Rishi Ganga running through the valley below. A small medical post is maintained by the temple board for trekkers. The first leg of the longer Neelkanth Base Camp trek (10 km total) starts here.
why_hidden: Most Char Dham pilgrims do the temple-Tapt Kund-Brahma Kapal triangle and leave the same afternoon. The Charan Paduka uphill path is not on the package-tour script and the 1.5-hour climb deters bus pilgrims.
best_time: May-June and September-October when the trail is dry. Closed November-April with the temple
how_to_reach: Trailhead is 200 m left of the main Badrinath temple courtyard. 3 km / 1.5 hours uphill on a stone-paved path; descent 1 hour.
tips: Free entry. Carry water and a windcheater — the rock platform is exposed. Trekking shoes recommended; the path is steep and slippery when wet. Avoid in early morning rain. Combine with Mata Murti temple in the afternoon for a complete Badrinath day. Altitude ~3,400 m; allow 24 hours of acclimatisation if you've come up fast from Joshimath.

name: Mata Murti Temple
description: A small temple on the right bank of the Alaknanda, 3 km from the main Badrinath temple, dedicated to Mata Murti — mother of the twin sages Nara and Narayan, the dual form of Vishnu enshrined at Badrinath. Once a year on Vaman Dwadashi (Bhadrapad/September), an annual fair sees the image of Uddhav carried in procession from the main Badrinath temple to Mata Murti's shrine, re-enacting the sons' visit to their mother.
why_hidden: It is on the Mana road, the same direction as Vasudhara Falls, but the package buses peel off at Mana village and skip the 1 km detour to Mata Murti. The temple has no on-site facilities and goes unmentioned in most yatra brochures.
best_time: May-October when Badrinath is open. Vaman Dwadashi (early-mid September) for the annual procession festival
how_to_reach: 3 km from Badrinath temple on the Mana road, before reaching Mana village. Walk (45 min one way), shared jeep (₹50 each), or self-drive — limited parking near the shrine.
tips: Free entry. Footwear off; modest dress. No restaurants or shops nearby — eat in Badrinath market first. Combine with Bheem Pul/Mana on the same outing if not already done. The Vaman Dwadashi fair is the only time the temple sees a real crowd — otherwise it's typically near-empty.

name: Bhalu Gaad Waterfall Trek
description: A 60-foot horseshoe-and-plunge waterfall reached by a 2 km forest trek from Dhari village, 10 km from Mukteshwar town. 'Bhalu Gaad' means Bear Stream in Kumaoni — the woods around the trailhead were known for Himalayan black bear sightings. The fall runs year-round; the rainbow that forms in the spray on sunny days has earned it the local name 'rainbow waterfall'. The 2 km trail crosses the stream twice and finishes with a brief boulder scramble.
why_hidden: Mukteshwar's tourist circuit is the temple-and-Chauli Ki Jali viewpoint loop — under 4 km total. The waterfall is 10 km out via Dhari and requires a 2 km hike, which most weekenders skip.
best_time: April-June for full flow with safe trails; September-November after monsoon for cleaner water. Avoid mid-monsoon (Jul-Aug) when the boulders are slippery
how_to_reach: 10 km from Mukteshwar via the Dhari road. Self-drive or taxi (₹600-900 round trip with 2-hour wait) to Dhari; park at the roadside shack. 2 km trek from there into the forest.
tips: Free entry. Local guide ₹200 from the shack — recommended only if you want to avoid wrong trails. Trekking shoes required. Carry water; no shops on the trail. Don't swim in the plunge pool (rocks below are slippery and unmarked). Allow 3-4 hours round trip from the parking.

name: Ramgarh — Tagore & Mahadevi Verma's Fruit Village
description: Known as the 'Fruit Bowl of Kumaon' for its peach, apricot, pear and apple orchards, Ramgarh is a small hill hamlet 20 km from Mukteshwar where Rabindranath Tagore composed sections of his work in the early 1900s. Mahadevi Verma — Hindi poet, 1982 Jnanpith laureate — wintered here for decades and conceived her story 'Lachma' from the village. Her house in Malla Ramgarh has been restored as a museum holding her writing desk, drafts, library and personal utensils.
why_hidden: Ramgarh is a literary site, not a scenic one — the orchards and Mahadevi Verma's house don't make travel-Instagram lists. Most Mukteshwar visitors have never heard of either Tagore's or Verma's connection to the area.
best_time: March-April for peach blossom; July-August for ripe peaches and apricots; October-November for clear Himalayan views
how_to_reach: 20 km from Mukteshwar via the Bhowali road. Self-drive or taxi (₹800-1,200 round trip with wait). The Mahadevi Verma museum is in Malla Ramgarh — ask locals; it's signposted in Hindi.
tips: Mahadevi Verma museum entry is nominal (₹20-50); typically open 10 AM-4 PM, closed Mondays — call ahead via Kumaon Mandal Vikas Nigam (KMVN) Ramgarh. Carry cash; no card machines. Buy peaches and apricots from village stalls in season. Combine with Mukteshwar temple for a literary-and-spiritual day.
